name: Separation of church and state
scope: The principle that religious organisations and the state are institutionally distinct: the state neither establishes, funds nor directs a church, and churches do not direct the state (disestablishment and the creation of a secular state). Defining sources (s1 encyclopedia, s2 Feldman, s3 Cord, s4 Swancara, s5 Urofsky) trace it from Roger Williams's 'wall of separation' (1644) and Locke's toleration through Virginia's disestablishment under Jefferson and Madison, the First Amendment's establishment clause and Jefferson's 1802 Danbury letter, to Everson and McCollum, so the scope is the church-state separation tradition as the sources state it, American-centred but not limited to it. It excludes the wider ideology of secularism and French laicite as separate subjects, and accommodationist or established-church positions except where the sources record what the separationist principle holds.

sources.usedFor: Scholarly history of the separation of church and state from antiquity to the modern Supreme Court.

sources.title: Separation of Church and State: Historical Fact and Current Fiction
sources.author: Robert L. Cord (1988)
sources.usedFor: Scholarly study of what Jefferson, Madison and the Supreme Court meant by the separation principle (an accommodationist critic of the strict reading).

sources.usedFor: A separationist's account of the principle and its sources. Also reproduces Madison's Memorial and Remonstrance (appendix) and Justice Black's Everson summary of the principle.

sources.title: A Wall of Separation: Two Hundred Years of Mr. Jefferson's Idea
sources.author: Melvin I. Urofsky and Philip E. Urofsky (Virginia Department of Education, 1987)
sources.usedFor: Educational history of the idea from the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom to modern court doctrine.

sources.title: The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution for Cause of Conscience Discussed (1848 Hanserd Knollys Society edition)
sources.author: Roger Williams
sources.usedFor: Williams's own key work: civil magistrates have no power over conscience or worship.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Williams's Bloudy Tenent (sixth proposition) says permission of the most pagan, Jewish, Turkish or antichristian consciences and worships should be granted to all, and the Everson summary Swancara cites says no person can be punished for professing religious beliefs or disbeliefs.

clerical-rule.rationale: The Memorial and Remonstrance warns that establishments erect a spiritual tyranny on the ruins of civil authority, and Williams rejects limiting the magistracy to church members (Bloudy Tenent, table of contents on the magistracy); church and civil authority stay separate.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Williams argues that the civil state of Israel is not a precedent for other nations and that the magistrate is no defender of the faith (Bloudy Tenent, 'Whether the civil state of Israel was precedential'); Madison holds religion is not within civil government's cognizance.

national-church-status.rationale: Madison's Memorial and Remonstrance, reproduced in Swancara's appendix, argues that the authority able to establish Christianity could establish one sect over all others and that ecclesiastical establishments have never guarded liberty; disestablishment is the principle's core.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Swancara's study (introduction, 'A Belated Return to the Constitution') sets out to defend the McCollum holding that giving religious instruction in or through public schools violates the Constitution.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Williams's Bloudy Tenent argues against putting blasphemers to death and against civil punishment for conscience, and Swancara (introduction) describes blasphemy laws as enacted to silence unbelievers, as part of what separation ends.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: The Memorial and Remonstrance (Swancara appendix) objects that the power to establish one sect of Christians over all other sects is the danger of any establishment; no sect or interpretation holds legal precedence.

religious-offensive-war.rationale: Williams's Bloudy Tenent says the blood spilt in wars for conscience is not required nor accepted by Christ and that false religion is fought only with the sword of the Spirit (preface; 'The direful effects of fighting for conscience').

restrict-conversion.rationale: Williams's Bloudy Tenent opposes civil force in matters of conscience and worship, and the Everson summary Swancara cites bars any government from forcing or influencing a person to profess or abandon a belief or disbelief.

school-vouchers.rationale: Swancara's introduction defends Rutledge's view that the First Amendment forbids every form of public aid for religion, and the Everson summary he reproduces says no tax in any amount can support religious institutions, which vouchers usable at any school would do.

separate-church-state.rationale: The encyclopedia states the establishment clause is often interpreted to require separation, and Swancara (introduction) defends Rutledge's reading in Everson that the First Amendment creates a complete and permanent separation of the spheres of religious activity and civil authority.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The Everson summary in Swancara's appendix says government cannot force or influence anyone to profess a belief or disbelief in any religion; Swancara defends Mrs. McCollum, an unbeliever, by neutrality, not by state promotion of unbelief.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Memorial and Remonstrance holds that religion is wholly exempt from the cognizance of civil government and Williams denies the magistrate any power over souls and worship (Bloudy Tenent); the principle keeps the two spheres separate rather than putting churches under the state.

summary: Separation of church and state holds that religious institutions and the civil government are distinct: the state does not establish, fund or direct a religion or religious instruction, no one is punished or compelled for belief or disbelief, and churches do not direct the state. The sources trace it from Roger Williams's wall between the garden of the church and the wilderness of the world, through Virginia's disestablishment and Madison's Memorial and Remonstrance, to the Everson and McCollum rulings.

notes: Answers rest on Williams's Bloudy Tenent (s6), Madison's Memorial and Remonstrance and the Everson summary as reproduced in Swancara (s4), and the encyclopedia (s1). Cord (s3) argues against the strict reading and answers nothing here; Feldman (s2) was searched for each theme. Themes searched: religion in schools, public funding, establishment, blasphemy and apostasy, clerical authority, religious war, conversion. Economy, ecology, technology, world and most liberty statements have no position in the sources.
